messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo transducer: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30 nF) and $R_{leak} = 20 \text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   $V_{oc} \approx 3.8 \text{ V}$ (at S1).
    *   Goal: Output $V_{out} = [4.5\text{V}, 5.5\text{V}]$, $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$, startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$, settled $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Operating conditions: S1-S6 (varying $I_p$, $f$, $C_p$, $R_L$).
    *   Reference design (FBR): Output too low for most cases ($V_{oc}$ is only 3.8V, whereas target is 4.5V-5.5V), and fails startup/settling.

    *   The open-circuit voltage amplitude is $\approx 3.8\text{V}$.
    *   A standard rectifier (FBR) cannot boost the voltage above the piezo's peak voltage.
    *   Since the target is $4.5\text{V} - 5.5\text{V}$, a **voltage boost** mechanism is mandatory.
    *   Standard piezo energy harvesting techniques for boosting include:
        *   **SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):** Uses a switch and an inductor to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the extrema, effectively increasing the voltage swing and extracting more energy.
        *   **SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction):** Similar to SSHI, but often uses a separate storage capacitor.
        *   **DC-DC Boost Converter:** Too complex/power-hungry for these $\mu\text{W}$ loads? No, the provided components include `SYNC`, `S`, `L`, `C`, `D`. A synchronous switch converter is essentially an SSHI-like circuit.

    *   To get $V_{out} > V_{oc}$, we need to use the inductor $L$ to invert the charge on $C_p$ or step up the voltage.
    *   **SSHI (Parallel SSHI):**
        *   $C_p$ is in parallel with the piezo source.
        *   An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ are connected in parallel to $C_p$.
        *   When the switch $S$ closes at the voltage peak, the energy in $C_p$ oscillates between $C_p$ and $L$.
        *   If the switch is opened at the right time (after a half-cycle of the $LC$ resonance), the voltage polarity across $C_p$ is reversed.
        *   The rectified current then flows into the storage capacitor $C_{out}$ at a higher voltage.

    *   **Wait, looking at the components again:**
        *   `SYNC` controller: closes switches at piezo voltage extrema.
        *   `S` switch: controlled by `SYNC`.
        *   `L` inductor.
        *   `D` diode.
        *   `C` capacitor.

    *   **Proposed Topology 1: SSHI-like boost (Parallel SSHI)**
        *   Piezo terminals: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   Rectifier: Since we want $V_{out} > V_{oc}$, we can't just use a bridge. However, we can use the SSHI flip to increase the voltage on the piezo terminals, then rectify.
        *   Actually, the simplest "boost" with the given components is to use a synchronous switch to invert the piezo voltage.
        *   Circuit:
            *   `pzp`, `pzn` connected to a full bridge rectifier.
            *   `S1` (switch) and `L1` (inductor) in parallel with the piezo.
            *   `G1` (SYNC) controls `S1` to flip the voltage.
            *   $C_{out}$ filters the output.
        *   *Correction:* A parallel SSHI typically uses the inductor to flip the voltage of $C_p$. If we use a full bridge, the voltage across the bridge is the piezo voltage. If we flip the piezo voltage, we effectively double the swing.
        *   *Better approach for SSHI:*
            *   Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
            *   The rectifier should be *after* the flip. But the flip happens *across* the piezo.
            *   Let's try: $L$ and $S$ connected to `pzp` and `pzn`. $S$ closes at peaks.
            *   Then use a rectifier to move the energy to $C_{out}$.
            *   Wait, if we use a bridge rectifier, the diodes will clamp the voltage. The SSHI flip must happen across $C_p$ *before* the rectifier or in a way that doesn't conflict.

    *   **Proposed Topology 2: SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction)**
        *   The charge is extracted from $C_p$ through an inductor $L$ to $C_{out}$.
        *   Circuit: Piezo (`pzp`, `pzn`) $\rightarrow$ Switch $S$ $\rightarrow$ Inductor $L$ $\rightarrow$ Diode $D$ $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$ (`out`, `0`).
        *   $S$ closes at the peak of $V_{pzp}-V_{pzn}$.
        *   $L$ allows the charge to flow to $C_{out}$ (boosting it).
        *   Wait, SECE usually needs two switches or a specific diode arrangement.
        *   Simplified SECE:
            *   `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `S1` $\rightarrow$ `L1` $\rightarrow$ `D1` $\rightarrow$ `out`.
            *   `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `S2` $\rightarrow$ `L2` $\rightarrow$ `D2` $\rightarrow$ `out`.
            *   `S1` closes at positive peak, `S2` at negative peak.
            *   This extracts charge from $C_p$ and pushes it into $C_{out}$ through $L$. Since $C_p$ is small and $C_{out}$ is large, the voltage is boosted.

    *   **Proposed Topology 3: Buck-Boost/Charge Pump variant (using the SYNC)**
        *   Use the `SYNC` as a boost converter controller.
        *   `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `S1` $\rightarrow$ `L1` $\rightarrow$ `D1` $\rightarrow$ `out`.
        *   `S1` closes to build energy in `L1`, then opens to discharge into `out`.
        *   However, the `SYNC` is triggered by the piezo's extrema. This is exactly what SSHI/SECE does.

    *   **Evaluating the SECE-like approach (Topology 2):**
        *   `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `S1` $\rightarrow$ `L1` $\rightarrow$ `D1` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        *   `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `S2` $\rightarrow$ `L2` $\rightarrow$ `D2` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        *   `G1` controls `S1` (edges: pos, phase: 0).
        *   `G2` controls `S2` (edges: neg, phase: 0).
        *   `L1`, `L2` values: Try $\sim 10-100\text{ mH}$? No, $L$ max is $10\text{ mH}$.
        *   $t_{on}$ for SECE: typically $\approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. For $L=10\text{ mH}, C_p=25\text{ nF}$, $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-7}} \approx 15\text{ }\mu\text{s}$. This is within the $1\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ limit? No, $10^{-7}..0.001$ s. $15\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ is $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ s. It's okay.

    *   **Evaluating the SSHI-like approach (Topology 1 - Parallel SSHI):**
        *   L and S in parallel with the piezo.
        *   A full bridge rectifier in parallel with the piezo.
        *   $C_{out}$ at the output of the bridge.
        *   The switch $S$ flips the voltage, and the bridge rectifies the result.
        *   $L$ and $S$ are connected to `pzp` and `pzn`.
        *   $S$ closes at both peaks. $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        *   This effectively doubles the voltage across the rectifier.
        *   $V_{out}$ will be $\approx 2 \times V_{oc} - 2 \times V_{diode} \approx 2 \times 3.8 - 0.5 \approx 7.1\text{V}$. This might exceed $5.5\text{V}$.
        *   We can use a Zener diode (`DZ33`) to clamp the output, but $V_{out\_min}$ is $4.5\text{V}$, so a 3.3V Zener is too low.
        *   *Correction:* The target is $4.5\text{V}-5.5\text{V}$. The SSHI voltage can be tuned by adjusting $t_{on}$ or using a different topology.

    *   **Comparing SSHI vs SECE:**
        *   SSHI (parallel) is generally more efficient for piezoelectric energy harvesting.
        *   SECE is simpler but can have higher losses.
        *   Let's try a modified SSHI:
            *   Instead of a full bridge, maybe a half-bridge? Or just a simple rectifier?
            *   Actually, a full bridge with SSHI should work, and the optimization will find the best $L$, $C_{out}$, and $t_{on}$ to keep $V_{out}$ within $[4.5, 5.5]$.

    *   **Wait, the reference FBR failed because $V_{out}$ was too low (3.3V).**
        *   The peak $V_{oc}$ is 3.8V. A bridge rectifier's output is $V_{peak} - 2 V_{diode} \approx 3.8 - 0.5 = 3.3\text{V}$. This matches the FBR results perfectly.
        *   To get $4.5\text{V}-5.5\text{V}$, we *must* boost.

    *   **Refining Topology 1 (Parallel SSHI):**
        *   Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   SSHI part: `L1` and `S1` in parallel with `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   Rectifier part:
            *   `D1`: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
            *   `D2`: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
            *   `D3`: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp` (anode `0`, cathode `pzp`)
            *   `D4`: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (anode `0`, cathode `pzn`)
            *   Wait, that's a full bridge. `D3`, `D4` are the return diodes.
            *   Actually, the standard FBR is:
                *   `D1`: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
                *   `D2`: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
                *   `D3`: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp`
                *   `D4`: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
                *   (This is not quite right. Let's use the prompt's bridge example: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`).
        *   SSHI components:
            *   `L1`: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `n1`
            *   `S1`: `n1` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
            *   `G1`: `SYNC` (edges: both, phase: 0, ton: 3e-5)
        *   Output: `C1` from `out` to `0`.

    *   **Refining Topology 2 (SECE):**
        *   `S1` from `pzp` to `n1`, `L1` from `n1` to `n2`, `D1` from `n2` to `out`.
        *   `S2` from `pzn` to `n3`, `L2` from `n3` to `n4`, `D2` from `n4` to `out`.
        *   `G1` (SYNC, edges: pos, phase: 0) controls `S1`.
        *   `G2` (SYNC, edges: neg, phase: 0) controls `S2`.
        *   `C1` from `out` to `0`.

    *   **Refining Topology 3 (Synchronous Boost / Inductor-based):**
        *   Let's try a "half-bridge" SSHI or a simple boost.
        *   Maybe a "Charge-Pump" like approach? No, we have an inductor.
        *   Let's try a simpler SSHI where the inductor is used to boost the voltage once per cycle.
        *   Wait, another option is a "synchronous rectifier" instead of diodes to reduce the $0.5\text{V}$ drop.
        *   But the $0.5\text{V}$ drop isn't the main problem; the $3.8\text{V}$ peak is.

    *   **Re-evaluating Topology 1 (Parallel SSHI):**
        *   `L1`+`S1` in parallel with piezo.
        *   FBR to `out`.
        *   This will boost the voltage across the bridge.
        *   If $t_{on}$ is tuned, we can reach $4.5\text{V}-5.5\text{V}$.
        *   $V_{out} \approx V_{oc} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \text{flip\_efficiency}}$.
        *   This is a well-known technique to increase the extracted energy and the voltage.

    *   **Re-evaluating Topology 2 (SECE):**
        *   `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `S1` $\rightarrow$ `L1` $\rightarrow$ `D1` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        *   `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `S2` $\rightarrow$ `L2` $\rightarrow$ `D2` $\rightarrow$ `out`
        *   This is essentially two boost converters acting at the peaks.
        *   It's very effective for boosting.

    *   **Comparing the two for the given constraints:**
        *   S2 (heavy load) and S4 (weak excitation) are the hardest.
        *   SSHI is typically more efficient for $C_p$ inversion.
        *   SECE is more direct for boosting to a storage cap.
        *   Let's propose both and a third one.

    *   **Topology 3: A variation of SSHI with a different rectifier.**
        *   Maybe a "half-wave" SSHI to avoid overvoltage?
        *   `L1` and `S1` in parallel with piezo.
        *   `D1` from `pzp` to `out`.
        *   `D2` from `0` to `pzn`. (Half-wave)
        *   This would reduce the average voltage, which might help stay under $5.5\text{V}$ while still boosting.
        *   *Wait*, if a full bridge is too much, a half-bridge might be better. But a full bridge is more efficient. The evolution strategy will tune $L$ and $t_{on}$ anyway.

    *   **Wait, let's check the components limit:** 16 components.
        *   SSHI-FBR: 4 diodes, 1 L, 1 S, 1 SYNC, 1 C = 8 components. (Well within limit).
        *   SECE: 2 diodes, 2 L, 2 S, 2 SYNC, 1 C = 9 components. (Well within limit).

    *   **Let's think about the "Startup" requirement ($t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$):**
        *   With a large $C_{out}$ (like $2.2\text{uF}$), $t_{up}$ might be slow.
        *   $t_{up} = \frac{C_{out} \cdot V_{out}}{I_{avg}}$.
        *   For $S1$, $I_{avg} \approx \frac{P}{V} = \frac{5\text{uW}}{5\text{V}} = 1\text{uA}$.
        *   $t_{up} \approx \frac{2.2\text{uF} \cdot 4.5\text{V}}{1\text{uA}} \approx 10\text{ seconds}$.
        *   **Wait!** $10$ seconds is way more than $0.4$ seconds.
        *   To get $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$, we need:
            1.  A much smaller $C_{out}$.
            2.  Much higher current.
        *   If $C_{out} = 10\text{ nF}$, then $t_{up} \approx \frac{10\text{nF} \cdot 4.5\text{V}}{1\text{uA}} \approx 45\text{ ms}$.
        *   But a small $C_{out}$ will lead to high ripple ($v_{pp}$).
        *   $v_{pp} \approx \frac{I_{load}}{f \cdot C_{out}}$.
        *   For $S2$, $I_{load} = \frac{5\text{V}}{1\text{M}\Omega} = 5\text{uA}$.
        *   $v_{pp} \approx \frac{5\text{uA}}{100\text{Hz} \cdot 10\text{nF}} = \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{10^{-6}} = 5\text{V}$. (Way too high).
        *   To get $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$, we need $C_{out} \ge \frac{5\text{uA}}{100\text{Hz} \cdot 0.05\text{V}} = \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{5 \times 10^{-3}} = 1\text{uF}$.
        *   So $C_{out}$ must be $\approx 1\text{uF}$.
        *   If $C_{out} = 1\text{uF}$, then $t_{up} = \frac{1\text{uF} \cdot 4.5\text{V}}{I_{avg}} \le 0.4\text{s} \implies I_{avg} \ge \frac{4.5\text{uC}}{0.4\text{s}} = 11.25\text{uA}$.
        *   This means we need to extract $11.25\text{uA}$ of average current.
        *   $P_{avg} = 11.25\text{uA} \cdot 4.5\text{V} \approx 50\text{uW}$.
        *   Is $50\text{uW}$ available?
            *   Piezo energy per cycle $E_{cyc} = \frac{1}{2} C_p V_{oc}^2$.
            *   $E_{cyc} = 0.5 \cdot 25\text{nF} \cdot (3.8\text{V})^2 \approx 180\text{nJ}$.
            *   At $100\text{Hz}$, $P_{max} = 180\text{nJ} \cdot 100\text{Hz} = 18\text{uW}$.
            *   With SSHI, you can extract more, but not $50\text{uW}$.
            *   Wait, maybe $V_{oc}$ is the *amplitude* of the *sine* current source?
            *   "The piezo is a sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with its capacitance $C_p$".
            *   Energy per half-cycle extracted by a perfect rectifier: $E = \int_{0}^{T/2} V \cdot I dt = \int \frac{I_p \sin(\omega t)}{\omega C_p} I_p \sin(\omega t) dt = \frac{I_p^2}{\omega C_p} \int \sin^2(\omega t) dt = \frac{I_p^2}{\omega C_p} \frac{T}{4} = \frac{I_p^2}{2\pi f C_p} \cdot \frac{1}{4}$.
            *   Wait, let's use the $V_{oc}$ formula provided: $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p)$.
            *   $E_{half-cycle} = \frac{1}{2} C_p V_{oc}^2$.
            *   $P_{avg} = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} C_p V_{oc}^2 \cdot f = C_p V_{oc}^2 f$.
            *   $P_{avg} = 25\text{nF} \cdot (3.8\text{V})^2 \cdot 100\text{Hz} = 36\text{uW}$.
            *   Still, $36\text{uW}$ is less than $50\text{uW}$.
            *   Let's re-calculate $I_{avg}$ for $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$.
            *   If $C_{out}$ is smaller, say $0.1\text{uF}$, then $I_{avg} \ge \frac{0.1\text{uF} \cdot 4.5\text{V}}{0.4\text{s}} = 1.125\text{uA}$.
            *   $P_{avg} = 1.125\text{uA} \cdot 4.5\text{V} \approx 5\text{uW}$.
            *   This is very achievable!
            *   So the key is to balance $C_{out}$ between $t_{up}$ (needs small $C_{out}$) and $v_{pp}$ (needs large $C_{out}$).
            *   For $S2$, $I_{load} = 5\text{uA}$. $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ requires $C_{out} \ge 1\text{uF}$.
            *   If $C_{out} = 1\text{uF}$, we need $I_{avg} \ge 11.25\text{uA}$.
            *   If $P_{avg} = 36\text{uW}$, then $I_{avg} = 36\text{uW} / 4.5\text{V} = 8\text{uA}$.
